Drone survey network · simulation study

SwarmNet

A team of drones must read 100 sensor points on a 600 m × 600 m farm and bring every reading back to base. Each drone can only talk to drones close by, and some drones break down mid-mission. Who should decide where each drone goes: one central computer, or the drones themselves?

The learned swarm is the trained network saved by the reported run (iteration 69); it picks each move by sampling from its choices, so a single farm can be luckier or unluckier than the average. At 80 m with no breakdowns this farm shows its main weakness: it surveys points twice and finishes far later. The charts below average over many farms.

How the study works

Four steps from farm to finding

step 1

Build the farm

Random survey points, a base at the bottom edge, drones with batteries and a radio range. Readings only count once they reach the base.

step 2

Make a trustworthy yardstick

The central planner with unlimited radio and no breakdowns is our central plan. It is checked against an exact solver before anything else runs.

step 3

Train a learned swarm

Every drone runs the same small neural network (graph attention), trained by trial and error with MAPPO. It may also hover as a radio relay.

step 4

Compare on the same farms

Each method flies the identical farms. The score is the gap: how much slower than our central plan, in percent.

Results · reported run, 3 farms per setting, 10 drones unless noted

What the experiments show

Short radio hurts, breakdowns hurt far more

The biggest lever: how fast a lost drone is noticed

A swarm drone cannot see a breakdown. It waits for silence before re-doing the lost drone's points. Drag to change the wait.

90 s

Did learning beat the simple rule?

Learned swarm minus nearest-task rule, on the same 15 farms per row. Left of zero means learning was faster. Bars show the 95% interval.

No. Every interval crosses zero. The network learned to stop relaying within 10 training rounds and ended up flying like the nearest-task rule.

More drones, same code

Trained on at most 10 drones, run on up to 30 without retraining. 120 m radio, one breakdown, 10 points per drone. Bars show the 95% interval.

The learned policy keeps working at 3× its training size. Our central plan stays flat at about 200 s from 10 to 30 drones, so the planner spreads the work properly.

Why the numbers can be trusted
✓Our plan matched an exact MILP solver on 6 of 6 small farms.
✓The same farm gives the same plan on every run.
✓No plan beats a mathematical lower bound.
✓No mission out of 231 beat our central plan.
✓The learned network copied the rule on 98.4% of decisions before training.
✓The best policy was picked on separate farms never used for results.
Limits of this study
  • 3 farms per setting: differences under about 10% are not established.
  • Our plan is near-optimal on small farms, not proven optimal on 100 points.
  • The central planner learns about breakdowns instantly and reaches every drone, so it is an optimistic reference.
  • Simple physics: constant speed, no wind, one base with no landing queue.
SwarmNet v1.4.1 · simulation study by Md Mehrab Hossain · code, notebook and full results in the project repository. Gap = (method's finish time ÷ our central plan's finish time − 1) × 100%. Our central plan = central planner with unlimited radio and no breakdowns, on the same farm.
